title: Adoption as Children
lead: Paul's picture of how God takes slaves and outsiders into his family and gives them the rights of children and heirs. The Greek word huiothesia comes from Greek and Roman law (Romans 8:15, 23; 9:4; Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 1:5). It is both a present gift and a hope still to come.

sections.b: Before Paul, Israel was called God's son: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22); "You are children of the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1). The king was God's son too: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14). The word "adoption" does not appear in the Hebrew Bible, but the idea of a chosen sonship does. Paul lists adoption first among Israel's gifts (Romans 9:4).

Paul's Greek word huiothesia ("placing as a son") was a legal term. In Rome a man could adopt another, often an adult and a son-in-law or relative, to carry on a family line and an estate; the emperor Claudius adopted Nero in AD 50 (Tacitus, Annals 12.25-26). An adopted son took a new family, a new name, and a claim on the inheritance, and his old debts were cleared. Paul takes this and says that God adopts slaves (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5-7), and that the Spirit's cry is the voice of the new child: "Abba, Father!"

Adoption is a present gift ("You received the Spirit of adoption as children," Romans 8:15) and a future hope ("we wait for adoption as children, the redemption of our bodies," Romans 8:23). The believer is already a child and heir and still waits for the inheritance. The Eastern churches read adoption with theosis; the Reformed churches give adoption its own chapter (Westminster Confession 12); Wesleyans link adoption with the witness of the Spirit.

John speaks of becoming children of God by birth (John 1:12-13; 1 John 3:1), not by adoption. Paul's language is of adoption. The two pictures are not in conflict; they come from different worlds. Church teaching has often joined them: regeneration (new birth) and adoption are two sides of the same gift.
